# The Night Train

There is a particular hour on a night train—somewhere past midnight, when the last conversations have faded and the corridor lights have dimmed to amber—when you understand that you exist in two places at once. You are lying in your narrow berth, and you are also nowhere at all. The country slides past the window in fragments: a lit farmhouse, a signal light bleeding red into the dark, the sudden black mouth of a tunnel. You are moving at ninety miles an hour and yet you have never been more still.

I think the night train might be the last honest form of travel left to us. Airplanes pretend that distance doesn't matter; they seal you into a white tube and deliver you, slightly dehydrated and morally compromised, to a place that feels suspiciously like where you started. Cars turn the journey into a chore, all windshield and obligation. But the night train admits what every traveler secretly knows: that going somewhere takes time, that the body must be carried through the dark, that distance is real and deserves to be felt.

Consider the economy of the sleeping compartment. Everything folds. The seat becomes a bed; the bed becomes a shelf; the washbasin hides behind a wooden panel like a shy animal. There is a lesson in this compression—a reminder that we need far less than we think we need. A blanket, a pillow, a hook for your jacket, a small reading light angled just so. For one night, your entire world is six feet long and three feet wide, and it is enough.

Then there is the democracy of it. On the night train, the banker and the backpacker are separated by nothing but a curtain. You hear each other breathing. You hear the man across the aisle snoring like a distant engine, and in the morning he will apologize, and you will say it was nothing, and both of you will mean it. Strangers share a table at breakfast while telegraph poles flick past the window, and by the time the coffee arrives you know things about each other that would take months to learn in any city: who snores, who reads late, who gets up in the night to stand at the window like a sentry.

Sleeping while moving is its own strange pleasure. The rhythm of the rails works on the body like a lullaby refined over two centuries of engineering. *Clickety-clack, clickety-clack*—the old jointed rails sang it plainly; modern welded track has smoothed the song down to a whisper, a long *shhhhh* like wind through wheat. Either way, the message is the same: keep going, keep going, keep going. It is the only lullaby that means something literal. Somewhere beneath you, steel is carrying you through the dark toward morning, and you can surrender to it completely in a way you can never quite surrender to a bed at home.

And then there is the waking at three a.m.—the best part, though few admit it. You surface from sleep without knowing why. The compartment is dark except for the blue glow of the corridor light seeping under the door. Outside, a town is passing: sodium lamps, a shuttered gas station, a church steeple against a sky just beginning to consider dawn. Someone in that town is awake too—you feel certain of it—and for a moment the train and the town and you are bound together in the same small hours. Then the town is gone, swallowed behind you, and you are alone again with the rails' low hymn. You do not check the time. Checking the time would break the spell. This hour belongs to no schedule.

Every night train arrives eventually, and arrival is bittersweet in a way that arrivals by plane never are. Because you didn't skip the distance—you traveled *through* it—you arrive already belonging, somehow, to the place. You watched the country change around you: the hills softening into plains, the architecture shifting brick by brick, the language changing on the station platforms. You crossed borders while asleep and woke up somewhere new. The city that receives you at dawn feels earned.

I wonder sometimes why we gave so much of this up. The great sleeper routes have been pruned back decade by decade, replaced by budget flights and high-speed lines that treat the night as an inconvenience to be eliminated. We optimized away the in-between. But the in-between is where the mind does its best work. There is a reason so many writers loved trains—de Beauvoir crossing Europe, Theroux making a career of it, Akhmatova waiting on Petersburg platforms. The train gives you exactly enough stimulation to occupy the surface of the mind while the depths churn undisturbed. Problems loosen. Memories surface unbidden. You remember a summer afternoon from childhood, a smell, a voice, and you cannot explain why the rocking of a carriage should unlock it, only that it does.

Maybe that's the real cargo of the night train. Not the passengers, not the freight rattling in the cars behind us, but this: the unhurried processing of a life. The dark outside the window is like the dark behind closed eyes—it invites the inward gaze. You lie there and take inventory without meaning to. People you miss. Decisions pending. Small gratitudes. The train carries them all at ninety miles an hour through the sleeping countryside, and by morning, somehow, they weigh less.

In the end, the night train is a machine for doing the one thing our age has nearly forgotten how to do: waiting well. It converts dead time into living time. It insists that the night is not empty but full of passage. And when you finally step onto the platform in the early light—stiff, rumpled, faintly grimy, carrying your small folded world under your arm—you understand that you haven't merely arrived somewhere. You've been somewhere the whole time, all night, all those hundreds of miles, and the place you were was the going itself.
